entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="2Chr.31.1">2Ch 31:1</reference> <hi type="italic">Destruction of the idols and the altars of the high places. Provisions for the ordering and maintenance of the temple worship, and the attendants upon it</hi>. - 2Ch 31:1. At the conclusion of the festival, all the Israelites who had been present at the feast (הנּמצאים כּל־שׂראל to be understood as in <reference osisRef="2Chr.30.21">2Ch 30:21</reference>) went into the cities of Judah, and destroyed all the idols, high places, and altars not only in Judah and Benjamin (the southern kingdom), but also in Ephraim and Manasseh (the domain of the ten tribes), utterly (עד־לככּה, cf. <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.10">2Ch 24:10</reference>), and only then returned each to his home; cf. 2Ki 18:4.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="2Chr.31.2">2Ch 31:2</reference> <hi type="italic">Restoration of order in the public worship, and of the temple revenues and those of the priests</hi>. - 2Ch 31:2. Hezekiah appointed the courses of the priests and Levites according to their courses, each according to the measure of his service (cf. Num 7:5, Num 7:7), viz., the priests and Levites (ולל לכה are subordinated to אישׁ in apposition by ל), for burnt-offerings and thank-offerings, to serve (to wait upon the worship), and to praise and thank (by song and instrumental music) in the gates of the camp of Jahve, i.e., in the temple and court of the priests; see on 1Ch 9:18.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="2Chr.31.4-2Chr.31.8">2Ch 31:4-8</reference> <div eID="gen6193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6194" type="x-p"/> The priests and Levites received their maintenance from the first-fruits (<reference osisRef="Exod.23.19">Exo 23:19</reference>; Num 18:12; <reference osisRef="Deut.26.2">Deu 26:2</reference>) and the tithes, which the people had to pay from the produce of their cattle-breeding and their agriculture (<reference osisRef="Lev.27.30-Lev.27.33">Lev 27:30-33</reference>, cf. with Num 18:21-24). Hezekiah commanded the people, viz., the inhabitants of Jerusalem, to give this portion to the Levites and priests, that they might hold themselves firmly to the law of Jahve, i.e., might devote themselves to the duties laid upon them by the law, the attendance upon the worship, without being compelled to labour for their subsistence; cf. Neh 13:10.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="2Chr.31.11-2Chr.31.12">2Ch 31:11-12</reference> <div eID="gen6198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6199" type="x-p"/> Then the king commanded to prepare cells in the house of God for the storing of the provisions. Whether new cells were built, or cells already existing were prepared for this purpose, cannot be decided, since הכין may signify either. Into these cells they brought the תּרוּמה, which here denotes the first-fruits (cf. <reference osisRef="2Chr.31.5">2Ch 31:5</reference>), the tithes, and the dedicated things, בּאמוּנה, with fidelity, cf. 2Ch 19:9. עליהם, over them (the first-fruits, etc.) the Levite Cononiah was set as ruler (inspector), and his brother Shimei as second ruler (משׁנה).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="2Chr.31.13-2Chr.31.14">2Ch 31:13-14</reference> <div eID="gen6199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6200" type="x-p"/> To them at their hand, i.e., as subordinate overseers, were given ten Levites, who are enumerated by name. Of the names, Jehiel and Mahath occur in <reference osisRef="2Chr.29.12">2Ch 29:12</reference> and 2Ch 29:14. בּמפקד is translated by the Vulg. <hi type="italic">ex imperio</hi>, better <hi type="italic">ex mandato Hizkiae</hi>. Azariah, the prince of the house of God, is the high priest mentioned in 2Ch 31:10. - To the fourteen Levites named in <reference osisRef="2Chr.31.13">2Ch 31:13</reference> and <reference osisRef="2Chr.31.14">2Ch 31:14</reference> was committed the oversight and storing of the first-fruits, tithes, and consecrated gifts. Besides these, there were special officers appointed for the distribution of them. - In <reference osisRef="2Chr.31.14-2Chr.31.19">2Ch 31:14-19</reference> these are treated of; <reference osisRef="2Chr.31.14">2Ch 31:14</reference> dealing with the distribution of the voluntary gifts of God, i.e., all which was offered to God of spontaneous impulse (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.38">Lev 23:38</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.12.17">Deu 12:17</reference>), to which the first-fruits and tithes did not belong, they being assessments prescribed by the law. Over the freewill offerings the Levite Kore, the doorkeeper towards the east (see on <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.18">1Ch 9:18</reference>), was set. His duty was to give (distribute) “the heave-offerings of Jahve,” i.e., that portion of the thank-offerings which properly belonged to Jahve, and which was transferred by Him to the priests (<reference osisRef="Lev.7.14">Lev 7:14</reference>; Num 5:9), and the “most holy,” i.e., that part of the sin and trespass offerings (<reference osisRef="Lev.6.10">Lev 6:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.6.22">Lev 6:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.7.6">Lev 7:6</reference>) and of the oblations (<reference osisRef="Lev.2.3">Lev 2:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.2.10">Lev 2:10</reference>) which was to be eaten by the priests in the holy place.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="2Chr.31.15-2Chr.31.16">2Ch 31:15-16</reference> <div eID="gen6200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6201" type="x-p"/> At his hand (ידו על = מיּד, <reference osisRef="2Chr.31.13">2Ch 31:13</reference>), i.e., under his superintendence, there were six Levites, enumerated by name, in the priests’ cities, with fidelity, “to give to their brethren in their courses, as well to the great as to the small” (i.e., to the older and to the younger), sc. the portion of the gifts received which fell to each. By the brethren in their courses we are to understand not merely the Levites dwelling in the priests’ cities, who on account of their youth or old age could not come into the temple, but also those who at the time were not on duty, since the Levites’ courses performed it by turns, only some courses being on duty in the temple, while the others were at home in the priests’ cities. The object to לתת, <reference osisRef="2Chr.31.15">2Ch 31:15</reference>, is not to be taken straightway from the objects mentioned with לתת in 2Ch 31:14. For the most holy gifts could not be sent to the priests’ cities, but were consumed in the holy place, i.e., in the temple. Nor can we confine לתת to the האלהים נדבות; for since the gifts of the people, laid up in the cells, consisted in first-fruits, tithes, and consecrated gifts (<reference osisRef="2Chr.31.11">2Ch 31:11</reference>), and special officers were appointed for the storing and distribution of them, the business of distribution could not consist merely in the giving out of freewill offerings, but must have extended to all the offerings of the people. When, therefore, it is said of the Levite Kore, in <reference osisRef="2Chr.31.14">2Ch 31:14</reference>, that he was appointed over the freewill offerings, to distribute the heave-offerings and the most holy, only his chief function is there mentioned, and the functions of the officials associated with and subordinated to him in the priests’ cities are not to be confined to that. The object to לתת, <reference osisRef="2Chr.31.15">2Ch 31:15</reference>, is consequently to be determined by the whole context, and the arrangements which are assumed as known from the law; i.e., we must embrace under that word the distribution of the first-fruits, tithes, and consecrated gifts, of which the Levites in the priests’ cities were to receive their portion according to the law. - In <reference osisRef="2Chr.31.16">2Ch 31:16</reference>, the b|מחלקות אחיהם of <reference osisRef="2Chr.31.15">2Ch 31:15</reference> is more closely defined by an exception: “Besides their catalogue of the men (i.e., exclusive of those of the male sex catalogued by them) from three years old and upward, namely, of all those who came into the house of Jahve to the daily portion, for their service in their offices according to their courses.” בּיומו דּבר־יום signifies, in this connection, the portion of the holy gifts coming to them for every day; cf. Neh 11:23. The meaning of the verse is: From those dwelling in the priests’ cities were excluded those who had come to perform service in the temple; and, indeed, not merely those performing the service, but also their male children, who were catalogued along with them if they were three years old and upward. Thence it is clear that those entering upon their service took their sons with them when they were three years old. These children ate in the place of the sanctuary of the portion coming to their parents.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="2Chr.31.17">2Ch 31:17</reference> <reference osisRef="2Chr.31.17">2Ch 31:17</reference> contains a parenthetic remark as to the catalogues. ואת, as <hi type="italic">nota accus</hi>., serves here to emphasize the statement which is added as an elucidation (cf. Ew. §277, <hi type="italic">d</hi>): “But concerning the catalogue of the priests, it was (taken, prepared) according to the fathers'-houses; and the Levites, they were from twenty years old and upwards in their offices in their courses.” All the duties were discharged by several courses. On the age fixed on, see 1Ch 23:27.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="2Chr.31.18">2Ch 31:18</reference> <div eID="gen6201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6202" type="x-p"/> The connection and interpretation of this verse is doubtful. If we take וּלחתיחשׂ as a continuation of ואת־התיהשׁ, <reference osisRef="2Chr.31.17">2Ch 31:17</reference>, it gives us no suitable sense. The addition, “and also to every priest and Levite was a larger or smaller portion given according to the catalogue” (Ramb., etc.), is arbitrary, and does not fully express the בּ before כּל־טפּם. Berth., on the other hand, correctly remarks, “After the parentheses in <reference osisRef="2Chr.31.16">2Ch 31:16</reference> and <reference osisRef="2Chr.31.17">2Ch 31:17</reference>, וּלחתיחשׂ may be taken as a continuation of לתת in <reference osisRef="2Chr.31.16">2Ch 31:16</reference>;” but the word itself he translates wrongly thus: The men were in the priests’ cities, also to register their children, etc., disregarding the construction of התיחשׂ with בּ. - From <reference osisRef="2Chr.31.19">2Ch 31:19</reference>, where the same construction recurs, we learn how to interpret בּכל־ט התיחשׁ: the catalogue = those registered in (of) all their children. According to this view, ולהתיחשׂ corresponds to the לאחיהם, <reference osisRef="2Chr.31.15">2Ch 31:15</reference> : to give to their brethren, ... and to the registered of all their children, their wives, and their sons and daughters, viz., to the whole multitude (sc., of the wives, sons, and daughters), i.e., as many of them as there were. This interpretation of the לכל־קהל seems simpler than with Schmidt and Ramb. to understand קהל to denote the coroporation of priests. There was therefore no one forgotten or overlooked; “for according to their fidelity (<reference osisRef="2Chr.31.15">2Ch 31:15</reference>) did they show themselves holy in regard to the holy,” i.e., they acted in a holy manner with the holy gifts, distributed them disinterestedly and impartially to all who had any claim to them.

 The connection and interpretation of this verse is doubtful. If we take וּלחתיחשׂ as a continuation of ואת־התיהשׁ, 2Ch 31:17 , it gives us no suitable sense. The addition, “and also to every priest and Levite was a larger or smaller portion given according to the catalogue” (Ramb., etc.), is arbitrary, and does not fully express the בּ before כּל־טפּם. Berth., on the other hand, correctly remarks, “After the parentheses in 2Ch 31:16 and 2Ch 31:17 , וּלחתיחשׂ may be taken as a continuation of לתת in 2Ch 31:16 ;” but the word itself he translates wrongly thus: The men were in the priests’ cities, also to register their children, etc., disregarding the construction of התיחשׂ with בּ. - From 2Ch 31:19 , where the same construction recurs, we learn how to interpret בּכל־ט התיחשׁ: the catalogue = those registered in (of) all their children. According to this view, ולהתיחשׂ corresponds to the לאחיהם, 2Ch 31:15 : to give to their brethren, ... and to the registered of all their children, their wives, and their sons and daughters, viz., to the whole multitude (sc., of the wives, sons, and daughters), i.e., as many of them as there were. This interpretation of the לכל־קהל seems simpler than with Schmidt and Ramb. to understand קהל to denote the coroporation of priests. There was therefore no one forgotten or overlooked; “for according to their fidelity ( 2Ch 31:15 ) did they show themselves holy in regard to the holy,” i.e., they acted in a holy manner with the holy gifts, distributed them disinterestedly and impartially to all who had any claim to them.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="2Chr.31.20-2Chr.31.21">2Ch 31:20-21</reference> <div eID="gen6203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6204" type="x-p"/> The conclusion of this account. Thus did Hezekiah in all Judah, and wrought in general that which was good and right and האמת before the Lord his God; and in every work that he commenced for the service of the house of God, and for the law and the commandment (i.e., for the restoration of the law and its commands), to seek his God, he did it with all his heart, and prospered. Sennacherib’s campaign against Judah and Jerusalem, and the annihilation of his whole army by the angel of the Lord. In 2 Kings 18 and 19, and Isa 36 and 37, we have two minute parallel accounts of this war, which threatened the existence of the kingdom of Judah, in both of which the course of this attack by the Assyrian world-power upon the kingdom of God is circumstantially narrated. The author of the Chronicle gives only a short narrative of the main events of the struggle; but, notwithstanding its brevity, supplies us with several not unessential additions to these detailed accounts. After stating that Sennacherib invaded Judah with the design of conquering the kingdom for himself (<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.1">2Ch 32:1</reference>), the author of the Chronicle described the preparations which Hezekiah made for the defence of the capital in case it should be besieged (<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.2-2Chr.32.8">2Ch 32:2-8</reference>). Then we have an account of Sennacherib’s attempts to get Jerusalem into his power, by sending his generals, who sought to induce the people to submit by boastful speeches, and by writing threatening letters to Hezekiah (<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.9-2Chr.32.19">2Ch 32:9-19</reference>); and, finally, of Hezekiah’s prayer to God for help, and the answer to his prayer - the wonderful annihilation of the Assyrian army (<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.20-2Chr.32.23">2Ch 32:20-23</reference>). The purpose of the chronicler in narrating these events was a didactic one: he wishes to show how God the Lord helped the pious King Hezekiah in this danger to his kingdom, and humbled the presumption of Sennacherib confiding in the might of his powerful army. For this purpose, a brief rhetorical summary of the main events of the struggle and its issues was sufficient. As to the facts, see the commentary on 2 Kings 18f. and Isa. 36f.  <chapter eID="2Chr.31"/> <div eID="gen6204" type="x-p"/>
